settings.headline: Numbing cream for laser, matched to the area.
settings.subhead: Laser covers everything from a small underarm session to full-face resurfacing, so the right choice depends on the area as much as the strength. Cream suits precise facial work; spray suits larger body zones where an even layer by hand is slow. Advanced is the strength most appointments call for. Here's how to choose.

settings.headline: Pick by the area, not the machine
settings.body: Laser appointments vary too widely for one answer — a quick underarm session and a full-face resurfacing aren't the same booking. The part that holds: match the format to the area (cream where the work is precise, spray where it's broad) and the strength to the session. The treatment area decides, not the laser brand or the clinic's marketing.

settings.matched: Shorter, routine appointments, smaller areas, and anyone starting out who wants to begin considered.
Longer or more sensitive sessions and larger areas — the one most people settle on for regular aesthetic work.

settings.headline: Match your numbing cream for laser to the session
settings.body: None of the three is "better" than another — each is formulated for a different kind of session. For laser, most appointments sit at Advanced.
settings.note: If you're between two, the lower one is usually the sensible start, and you can move up next time.

settings.headline: Numbing for laser, by area and strength

settings.heading: Cream or spray for laser?
settings.body: Decide by the area. Cream suits precise, contained facial work — a focused application on a controlled zone. Spray suits larger body areas, where covering the surface evenly by hand is slow. Gel isn't the laser format — it's for precise facial work like microneedling and SPMU. Same strengths across cream and spray; the area picks the format.

settings.heading: Before you buy: the bit most sellers skip
settings.body: Some laser technicians prefer you to arrive without numbing applied — a few use your feedback on skin temperature and sensation to calibrate the treatment as they go. Others are happy for you to prepare beforehand. Clinics and machines vary, so a quick message to your practitioner before your appointment is the thing that settles it — not a rule we can give you from here.

settings.question: Does laser hair removal hurt?
settings.answer: Most people feel a quick sting or a hot-elastic-band snap with each pulse, and numbing is a cosmetic preparation that supports comfort. How much you feel varies with the area, the machine, your skin and the coarseness of the hair. Many find prepared skin more comfortable than unprepared, but check with your technician first — some prefer you to arrive without numbing applied.

settings.question: Which strength should I use for laser?
settings.answer: Advanced suits most laser appointments. Clinical for shorter or smaller sessions; Professional for full-face resurfacing or the most intensive body work. The area matters more than the type of laser.

settings.question: Cream or spray for laser?
settings.answer: Cream for the face and precise areas; spray for the body and larger zones. The format follows the surface area, not personal preference.

settings.question: Can I use it before IPL?
settings.answer: Yes — IPL is part of the laser category Senseless is made for. Follow your practitioner's guidance, and check whether they'd rather you arrive without numbing applied.

settings.question: When do I apply it?
settings.answer: Ahead of your appointment, leaving it on for the window your practitioner sets — follow the product guidance and your practitioner's protocol for the laser they use.

settings.question: Do I need to patch test?
settings.answer: Yes — patch test 24 hours before on the inside of your wrist or behind your ear, and don't use it if you see any reaction. Take extra care on sensitive or recently-treated skin.

settings.heading: Not sure which to choose?
settings.body: Answer three quick questions — treatment, skin and session length — and we'll point you to the format and strength we'd reach for.
